title: Personalized relapse prediction in Alcohol Use Disorder
text:
We will collect data in a large treatment cohort [N=200 Alcohol Use Disorder (AUD), >40% female; enrollment
at 2-5 weeks into treatment,; N=100 controls] using a multi-method approach (personality, neurocognition,
clinical assessments, task/resting fMRI brain function) to assess function across three different domains
(reward reactivity, aversive reactivity, executive control). We hypothesize that relapse in AUD is driven by
different combinations of these three factors in each individual. We will test this hypothesis by using novel
analytical approaches to parse out individual heterogeneity in the multivariate patterns of impairments
underlying relapse in dependent alcohol users.

title: Role of Force-directed Lipid Metabolism in the Endothelial-to-Hematopoietic Transition
text:
Blood flow is essential for the production of hematopoietic stem cells (HSCs) from hemogenic endothelium during
embryonic development, and directs a series of transcriptional and metabolic changes that promote the
endothelial-to-hematopoietic transition. This proposal describes a focused, targeted and disciplined effort
employing the zebrafish model system to identify candidate endothelial lipid metabolites that are regulated by
hemodynamic forces and control HSC production in vivo. Results from this proposal will generate a toolbox of
zebrafish lines to allow for the cell-type specific interrogation of metabolic pathways controlled by force, yield an
atlas of candidate players that may enhance efforts to recapitulate developmental processes in the generation
of clinically useful HSCs in the dish, and provide preliminary data for the future R01 applications of the
Investigator.

title: Sex differences in somatostatin cell dynamics and exploratory behavior after adolescent binge drinking in mice
text:
Adolescent alcohol exposure is associated with adult behavioral deficits, such as increased risk-taking and
psychiatric disorders. I will examine how adolescent binge drinking causes sex differences in prelimbic
somatostatin neuronal regulation of behavior, and I will test the therapeutic potential of targeting this population
for prevention of adolescent alcohol’s long-term consequences. This application combines novel technological
approaches with understudied questions surrounding adolescent binge drinking and its lasting effects on cortical
microcircuits.

title: Fibrosis of the Lower Esophageal Sphincter in Achalasia
text:
There are several factors that likely contribute to healthy esophageal muscular function. Yet, our understanding
of diseases of the esophageal muscle has thus far been limited to mechanisms of neurally-mediated
contraction and relaxation of the esophageal muscle. The goal of this clinical trial is to study the impact of the
biomechanical properties such as muscle fibrosis towards the impairments in muscle function in achalasia with
the goal of identifying novel treatment targets and improving patient outcomes.

title: Single-cell congruence evaluation and selection of cancer models towards precision medicine
text:
Cell lines and other cell-based cancer models are extensively utilized in cancer research as substitutes for
human studies, expediting biological and clinical findings. In this project, we aim to quantify congruence and
authentication to select the most representative cancer model using molecular profiles from omics and single-
cell technologies. This selection will facilitate research towards understanding tumor mechanisms,
personalized treatment, and accelerated drug discovery.

title: Allosteric Regulation of KCNH Channels
text:
Abnormal electrical activity in the heart can cause life-threatening arrhythmias and sudden cardiac death. This
research investigates how molecular movements within the hERG1 potassium channel regulate cardiac rhythm
and how antibody-based tools can restore normal electrical function. The findings will inform new strategies for
preventing and treating arrhythmias at their molecular source.

title: VMH SF1 neurons-originated sympathetic circuits modulating iWAT and iBAT
text:
Precise control of adipose tissue function is crucial in modulating energy balance and glucose homeostasis. This
research project will test novel concepts that molecularly distinct subsets of VMH SF1 neurons modulate white
adipose tissue lipolysis and brown adipose tissue thermogenesis through different sympathetic circuit pathways,
and that Ca2+-permeable AMPA receptor (CP-AMPAR) and tumor necrosis factor-a (TNFa) signals in VMH SF1
neurons contribute to the development of high-fat diet (HFD)-induced obesity (DIO). The information to be
collected from this project will reveal expression of specific genes in VMH SF1 neurons modulating iWAT or
iBAT, and demonstrate that attenuating CP-AMPAR and TNFa signals in VMH SF1 neurons can be an attractive
strategy for the treatment of DIO in HFD-fed mice.

title: DLL3-targeted IL18-secreting CAR T cells in Small Cell Lung Cancer
text:
Small cell lung cancer (SCLC) is a difficult-to-treat malignancy that is universally lethal in the
advanced stage. Treatment options are limited and demonstrate modest efficacy and considerable
toxicity. The innovative T cell therapy explored in this proposal is likely to have fewer side effects than
current interventions, does not require preparative chemotherapy, and may provide greater relief, with
the possibility of long-term remission - this approach may reduce mortality and improve quality-of-life
for patients with SCLC and in the future, other DLL3-expressing cancers.

title: Maternal and fetal genetic contributions to the development of maternal gestational diabetes.
text:
Gestational diabetes affects nearly 3 million U.S. pregnancies annually, imposing substantial public health
burdens through increased rates of type 2 diabetes, cardiovascular disease, and obesity that persist across
generations. Current prevention and treatment strategies achieve only modest success because they rely
exclusively on maternal risk factors, missing critical fetal genetic contributions that this research will identify
using cutting-edge high-throughput genomic methods. By establishing which pregnancies face elevated risk
through integrated maternal-fetal genetic profiling, this work will enable earlier targeted interventions, including
lifestyle modifications and potential placental therapies, that can reduce diabetes incidence in millions of
mothers and their children.

title: Identifying spike correlates driving merbecovirus pathogenesis
text:
In this proposal, we examine mutations in the S1/S2 loop of coronaviruses. Responsible for protease
interaction and spike cleavage, we explore how motifs in this region contribute to coronavirus, infection,
pathogenesis, and transmission. Understanding these changes and their mechanisms of action will provide
critical insights necessary to understand and mitigate the next emergence event.

title: Resource Sharing Core
text: The resource sharing core of the proposed ROBIN U54 center project will consist of experienced faculties in the Department of Radiation Oncology at the University of Maryland and Department of Pathology at Cornell University. A long history of collaboration already exists between the members of this Core and investigators on the main projects. The Core will provide centralized and cost-effective support to the projects by providing a wide range of data needed for the projects, including multi-omics, imaging, and dosimetry data in radiation oncology. The core service provides a crucial way to coordinate data collection, storage, and sharing to ensure data from the main projects are analyzed consistently and efficiently. There are three specific aims for this core: Aim 1. Provide state-of-the-art methods for multi-omics data analysis and storage to project researchers. The core research team has extensive experience in the wide array of genome-wide analyses that are planned, and it will therefore provide all necessary expertise for the correct and efficient pre-processing and analysis of the multi-omics data generated within each project across the U54 ROBIN center. Sharing the multi-omics data within the U54 ROBIN Center will leverage the Cloud Data Warehouse at Cornell, which enables the research use of integrated data from multiple clinical systems and analytical platforms. Aim 2: Develop tools and infrastructure for extraction, analysis, and storage of imaging and dosimetry data in radiation therapy. We will develop tools and databases for extracting, analyzing, and storing the data that are unique for radiation therapy, including both imaging data (CT, MRI, PET and CBCT) and dosimetry data (3D dose distribution, dose volume histogram for target and organs at risk). We will also develop techniques for image quality enhancement as well as radiomics analysis on both imaging and dosimetry data. A graphical user interface (GUI) will be developed to facilitate the extraction and analysis of the multi-dimensional data. Aim 3. Provide cloud-based platforms and infrastructures for resource sharing across institutions. The cloud-based Data Warehouse will be used to store and share multi-omics data at Cornell University, while the cloud-based Flywheel software will be used to store and share imaging and dosimetry data at the University of Maryland. The database systems will be interfaced with other electronic data systems, and procedures will be instituted to ensure data quality, integrity, and confidentiality. The systems will be implemented to enable inter-project collaborations and those with external collaborators in the future. The data and tools will be made publically available with transparency under a fee-based service model. In summary, the resource sharing core will have an integral role in the scientific development, execution, and analysis of all projects. Core investigators are committed to working closely with project PIs and investigators to assess any issues that may adversely affect resource sharing and implement all necessary changes as the projects progress.

title: Investigating the Functional Impact of AD Risk Genes on Neuro-Vascular Interactions
text:
Significant progress in identifying genes that accelerate or slow Alzheimer disease now leads to a critical
question, how do these genes act to alter disease progression? We will focus our studies on the impact of these
genes on brain vascular pathology which is present in almost all Alzheimer’s disease patients and has been
shown to be an early driver of loss of brain function. Because hundreds of genes are potentially involved, we will
use large-scale cutting-edge gene editing and screening methods for initial analysis. This will create a prioritized
list of genes for focused functional studies in human stem cell models and mouse models. The goal is to identify
early events leading to vascular pathology that can be targeted to combat Alzheimer’s disease.

title: Neural mechanisms of respiratory dysfunction in old age
text:
An increasing number of elderly individuals is afflicted by age-related motor dysfunction with loss of the ability
to generate the higher forces necessary for airway clearance, which places them at risk for respiratory
complications in old age. The proposed studies will yield new mechanistic understanding of the role that
autophagy impairment plays in the selective loss of higher force motor units. We expect to discover novel
mechanistic targets to reverse the effects of aging on respiratory motor function.

title: CRISPR-Cas9 base editing approaches to discover ubiquitination events promoting flavivirus infection
text:
Ubiquitination is a prominent type of protein modification that can alter protein functions. Modern approaches
can measure tens of thousands of ubiquitination events, but it is difficult to determine which of those are
biologically meaningful. This project will develop new genome-editing approaches to better understand the
functions of ubiquitination events in the context of WNV infection, which can help better understand the pathways
required by the virus for replication and potential weaknesses that can be exploited for therapeutic development.

title: Inter-metastatic divergency in small cell lung cancer; implications for the design of future immunotherapies
text:
These studies will define the role and heterogeneity of neoantigens and tumor
microenvironmental immune cells in SCLC; a poorly characterized disease, due in part to its
aggressiveness and challenges with presentation at a metastatic stage, which prevents tissue
collection to address biological questions.
Our work will generate a mechanistic rationale for more effective immunotherapies that target the
diversity of SCLC, which we will leverage to design ensuing clinical trials at Moffitt Cancer Center.

title: Breath Biomarkers of Disease and Health Outcomes (BREATHE OUT)
text: Dr. Jacob Mey is a productive early career scientist applying for this COBRE Research Project Leader position to support his transition to an independent research career. He has a strong clinical nutrition (registered dietitian) and metabolism background, with a history of growth and productivity throughout the evolution of his research career. His established expertise in metabolic disease and recent novel findings identifying breath profiles of malnutrition have directed his interest towards a major clinical need: improving screening and monitoring of metabolic health — a priority directly relevant to the mission of the Metabolic Basis of Disease COBRE. Metabolic diseases, particularly type 2 diabetes, affect millions of Americans, yet a significant portion of the population remains undiagnosed due to barriers associated with current blood-based screening methods. The exhaled breath represents an innovative, non-invasive biological specimen to identify biomarkers of metabolic health, with potential for the development of a point-of-care screening tool. The objective of this project, "Breath Biomarkers of Disease and Health Outcomes" (BREATHE OUT), is to identify novel breath biomarkers of metabolic disease and validate their predictive capacity against gold-standard methods. Specific Aim 1 will determine if breath biomarkers can distinguish between distinct human metabolic phenotypes, with groups ranging from optimal health, at-risk/obesity, and overt metabolic disease/type 2 diabetes. This aim will utilize advanced bioinformatics tools to identify and characterize unique breath signatures related to metabolic health. Specific Aim 2 will validate the clinical utility of these breath biomarker profiles by comparing them to the gold-standard hyperinsulinemic-euglycemic clamp. This aim will leverage an ongoing NIH-funded clinical trial to assess if breath profiles predict insulin sensitivity more accurately than traditional blood-based markers. This COBRE-supported research builds upon Dr. Mey’s prior work and expertise and will provide critical proof-of-concept data to support future R01 applications aimed at translating breath analysis into clinical practice to reduce the burden of undiagnosed metabolic disease. This COBRE RPL position can play a pivotal role in Dr. Mey’s career development, enabling him to merge his early successes in both metabolic research and breath profiling to the high-impact field of metabolic disease diagnostics. The position provides essential protected time and access to expert mentorship and facilities, specifically the COBRE’s Bioinformatics and Computational Biology Core lead by Dr. Ghosh, enabling the application of sophisticated machine learning to high-dimensional datasets. Ultimately, this support will facilitate the generation of critical proof-of-concept data required to secure competitive R01 funding, establishing Dr. Mey as an independent investigator at the forefront of non-invasive metabolic health screening.

title: MPZL3 as a Therapeutically Targetable Mitochondrial Regulator of Sebaceous Gland Homeostasis and Sebum Production
text:
While sebaceous glands in our skin secrete an oily film (sebum) for skin lubrication, have multiple other
indispensable functions, and are involved in many skin diseases, it is still quite unclear how they are regulated.
Therefore, we aim to identify the role of a powerful regulatory protein located in mitochondria, the energy
power houses of our cells, called MPZL3, in regulating sebaceous gland function, using state-of-the-art mouse
and human skin research tools. Besides helping us to better understand how healthy sebaceous gland
functions are regulated, the innovative skin research focusing on MPZL3 proposed here also promises to
identify novel drug targets for more effective and better-tolerated treatment of human skin diseases with
prominent sebaceous gland abnormalities such as acne, dry skin, scarring alopecia (hair loss) and sebaceous
carcinoma.

title: Defining P. falciparum resistance to artemisinin-based combination therapies
text:
The treatment of malaria is vitally dependent on artemisinin-based combination therapies (ACTs), yet their
continued efficacy is threatened by the emergence and spread of drug-resistant strains of the causative agent,
the parasite Plasmodium falciparum. Here we test the hypothesis that the emergence of K13 mutations in Africa
will cause artemisinin resistance, but with a fitness cost that is likely to hinder its dissemination in high-
transmission settings. We will also define determinants of resistance ACT partner drugs, providing molecular
markers to inform regional malaria treatment and control strategies designed to mitigate the impact of multidrug
resistance in Africa.

title: SysTAMatic mouse model toolbox to disentangle signal transduction pathways
text:
The crucial biological importance of the TYRO3, AXL and MERTK receptor tyrosine kinases (TAM RTKs) in
maintaining the homeostasis of a number of tissues and organs and their involvement in diseases including
chronic inflammatory diseases, cardiovascular diseases, neurodegenerative diseases and cancer
notwithstanding, an understanding of their contextual effector functions remains elusive. Unlike traditional gene
knockout and gain-of-function approaches heretofore employed that cannot disentangle the pleiotropic signaling
downstream the TAM RTKs and their involvement in at least two principal cellular effector functions –
phagocytosis of dead cells and anti-inflammatory signaling, here we propose to generate and test a series of
mouse models by systematically substituting individual tyrosines by phenylalanine in the intracellular domain of
TAM RTKs to specifically disable a single axis of signal transduction. These mouse models will not only comprise
an essential toolkit that will help resolve a number of paradoxes and conundrums thrown up by loss-of-function
and gain-of-function studies because of their inherent limitation to discern between TAM RTK-driven
phagocytosis and anti-inflammatory signaling, but also greatly improve our mechanistic understanding of the
specific functional activities of these receptors to inform the design of more precise targeted therapies for
diseases associated with TAM RTKs.

title: ATTACH: A platform for rapid and unbiased discovery of antigen-specific T cells to advance precision immunotherapy
text:
ATTACHbio has developed a novel platform called Assessment of T-cells Tethered to Antigen Class I
Histocompatibility (ATTACH) for unbiased isolation of therapeutic T-cells directly from patient-derived tumor
samples, without requiring prior antigen knowledge. This Phase I project aims to demonstrate proof-of-concept
for ATTACH in non-small cell lung cancer by isolating tumor-reactive T-cells and evaluating their efficacy both
in vitro and in vivo. The experiments performed refine the platform to support personalized immunotherapy
development to advance scalable, antigen-agnostic T-cell therapies for cancer.
